metric.why: Announced megawatts are the leading indicator for land, power, and equipment demand. The published numbers come almost entirely from commercial research firms; this site links to who publishes them rather than republishing figures it cannot verify.
metric.definition: Capacity in permitting, planned, or under construction per market, the standard unit for comparing data center booms across regions.

reading.body:
Announced megawatts in permitting, planning, or construction reveal which regions are preparing to supply AI's power demands over the next several years, and therefore which will house the compute first.

The construction pipeline is upstream of everything else. Servers need buildings. Buildings need power connections. Power connections need years of planning, permitting, and grid upgrades. By tracking announced capacity before it energizes, you see where AI infrastructure investment is actually going, not where it has already landed. A region announcing 500 megawatts of data center construction is committing to the land, equipment, and electrical work required to support that load.

These numbers come almost entirely from commercial research firms rather than regulatory filings or utility data. This means the pipeline reflects what the industry is willing to make public, which tends to be major announcements by large operators. Smaller builds, confidential expansions, and regional projects may not appear. The data covers market activity, not the full scope of buildable capacity or regulatory approval timelines.

For AI scaling, the construction pipeline is the binding constraint. Compute grows at software speed. Power infrastructure grows at construction speed. Where the pipeline is thin, AI expansion will stall regardless of chip availability or cooling technology, because the buildings and grid simply will not be ready.
